title: Drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
hookLine: only Luke tells of the angel and the sweat like drops of blood

lines: OUT OF THE CITY, AFTER SUPPER.
A PLACE HE WENT AS ACCUSTOMED.
cards: It's late, and the supper is over. Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, to a place Luke says he went as he was accustomed. Somewhere he'd prayed before.
A chair by a window, a corner of a church, a walk taken when something is too heavy: some people keep a place like that. He tells the disciples to pray that they don't enter into temptation.
Then he goes on a little further, about a stone's throw, and kneels down.

teach.b: He prays: "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." The chalice is the cup of suffering ahead. He asks honestly for it to pass, then hands the decision over.

Then Luke gives two details no other Gospel has: "And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony, he prayed the longer. And his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground."

teach.h: AN ANGEL, AND THE AGONY DEEPENS.
teach.b: The angel comes, and the agony deepens. The angel doesn't take the cup away; the angel helps him drink it. In Luke's picture, strength from heaven isn't an exit.

teach.h: AGONIA: THE STRAIN BEFORE THE RACE.
teach.b: Agony, in Luke's Greek, is agonia, a word that could describe an athlete's strain before a contest, as well as deep anguish. And the sweat is as drops of blood: like.
Readers have long debated whether Luke means real blood or heavy, dark drops; the text doesn't settle it. Some early manuscripts of Luke don't have these two verses.
The Church receives them as Scripture, and they're in the Latin Vulgate and the Douay. And the disciples?
He finds them sleeping for sorrow.

teach.h: HIS SWEAT AS DROPS OF BLOOD.
teach.b: Luke is gentle: grief knocked them out.

Catholics pray this moment as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, the Agony in the Garden, and some keep a holy hour, remembering that in Matthew and Mark, Jesus asks his friends to watch one hour with him.

how: Catholics pray the Agony in the Garden as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary, and some keep a holy hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, especially on Holy Thursday night.

o: the cup of suffering Jesus asked to pass
the garden where Jesus prayed that night
anguish, like an athlete's strain before a race

games.q: on the Mount of Olives — tap the pairs.
p: the strain of a contest before the race

after the angel came, being in an agony, he prayed the longer.

Luke 22:43–44 has no parallel in the other Gospels.
Luke blames the disciples harshly for sleeping
he says they were sleeping for sorrow.

games.q: you're kneeling alone, a stone's throw from your friends, and the suffering ahead is terrible. what do you pray?
o: take it away, whatever it costs.
if you will, remove it; but not my will, but yours.
games.why: he asks honestly for the cup to pass, and hands the decision to the Father. then an angel comes to strengthen him.

practice: Bring to mind someone in a terrible hour right now: a frightening diagnosis, a court date, an addiction, a night in an emergency room, a grief with no bottom.
You can't take the cup away, but you can keep watch, staying with them in your mind the way the disciples were asked to. If you pray, ask that they be strengthened, as he was.

wordCard.voice: Agonia. Luke's word for Jesus' struggle on the Mount of Olives, his sweat like drops of blood, an angel strengthening him to go on. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: agony, the strain and struggle of a contest; Luke's word for Jesus in the garden.

carryVoice: Your line: an angel strengthened him. Not an exit, but company in the hour. Until tomorrow.
